title: Colored Graph Signal Diffusion Models

paper.title: Colored Graph Signal Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Standard diffusion processes with isotropic noise corruption are not spectrally neutral. They inherit a coarse-to-fine generation hierarchy from the nonuniform data spectrum, because each frequency band loses signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at its own rate. For signals on a graph, the relevant spectrum is that of the graph shift operator (GSO). A natural construction, therefore, builds both the diffusion dynamics and the denoiser from graph filters of the GSO, and any such design also takes a position on this hierarchy. We expose this hierarchy as a tunable axis through a family of colored score-based diffusions. Fixing the terminal prior to a Gaussian colored by the GSO couples the drift and diffusion through a positive spectral rate, which acts as a clock for each graph-frequency band. The clock sets when a band loses and recovers information, and the forward processes of standard and certain graph-aware diffusions appear as members of this family. A GSO-valued EDM preconditioning splits the denoiser into an analytic Wiener head that carries the Gaussian second-order structure and a graph neural network (GNN) that learns the remaining non-Gaussian dependencies. Numerical experiments show that colored diffusions reach a given generation quality in far fewer sampling steps than standard diffusion.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Signals defined on graph-structured domains arise in sensor, traffic, financial, and physiological applications [ 16 ] . Recent works generate such signals with diffusion or flow models, incorporating the graph topology through graph neural network parametrizations of the learned dynamics [ 23 , 24 , 19 , 20 ] . The forward process itself, however, has largely remained isotropic. These models, therefore, barely exploit the spectral anisotropy that is inherent to diffusion models and that the graph also supplies. The inherent anisotropy is visible in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Standard diffusion injects spectrally flat (white) noise, whereas smooth graph signals and many natural signal modalities concentrate their energy at low to moderate frequencies [ 25 ] . High-frequency components, therefore, become noise-dominated earlier and are recovered later by the reverse (generative) process [ 7 , 18 ] . Standard diffusion thus inherits a coarse-to-fine generation hierarchy from the data spectrum. This is often a useful inductive bias, but it is determined by the spectral energy distribution rather than being tailored to the generation task. This motivates treating the spectral hierarchy as a design choice. Graph-aware diffusions (GAD) [ 19 ] advance both the spectral and graph-aware axes together. They combine a time-warped heat process with a Laplacian-parametrized Gaussian Markov random field prior and read the reverse process as graph signal denoising. The Fourier-space analysis of [ 7 ] relates unequal frequency SNRs to high-frequency generation errors and proposes EqualSNR diffusion to reduce this imbalance. Blurring, heat-dissipation, and fitted spectral schedules provide related alternatives in image, covariance, and prescribed transform bases [ 18 , 9 , 4 , 26 , 13 , 2 ] . In this paper, we introduce a family of colored diffusions for approximately stationary graph signals on symmetric graph shift operators (GSOs). The GSO may encode known graph structures or be estimated from data, as in covariance graphs. We fix the high-noise prior to a Gaussian whose covariance is colored by the graph operator. This ties the drift and diffusion, and leaves one functional degree of freedom, a positive spectral rate that acts as a clock for each graph-frequency band and determines when that band loses and recovers information. The hierarchy thus becomes a design choice decoupled from the prior while standard diffusion and the GAD processes become special cases with a common spectral reading. The same principle applies to our denoiser design. Matrix-valued EDM preconditioning yields an analytic Wiener head for the Gaussian second-order structure, leaving a nonlinear graph neural network (GNN) body to learn the remaining non-Gaussian and cross-frequency dependencies. Notably, every forward, preconditioning, and reverse operator is a matrix function of the graph shifts that can be applied by matrix–vector products without eigendecomposition. On fMRI and METR-LA datasets, we present extensive ablations across clock shapes, graph shifts, and sampling budgets. We demonstrate that spectral coloring improves low-step generation. We observe that the colored prior and Wiener head carry most of the gain, and the clock shape has a smaller and less uniform effect.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Datasets and benchmarks. The fMRI dataset contains n = 1,190 n=1{,}190 frames on d = 360 d=360 cortical parcels, taken from the Human Connectome Project [ 6 ] . We use the covariance GSO 𝐒 = 𝐂 ^ n + τ ​ 𝐈 {\mathbf{S}}=\widehat{{\mathbf{C}}}_{n}+\tau{\mathbf{I}} with τ = 0.01 \tau=0.01 [ 21 ] . We cut five folds at random over frames, training on 952 and testing on the 238 held out. The METR-LA panel [ 14 ] contains n = 21,286 n=21{,}286 frames from d = 153 d=153 traffic sensors. Its train and test split is performed similarly with five folds, which are contiguous in time and separated by a one-day purge. On fMRI, all colored arms use q ⁡ ( λ ) = λ q(\lambda)=\lambda , and the GSO-valued EDM preconditioning of Section 2 . We compare a flat clock, corresponding to whitened VP, with four pinned clocks from ( 13 )–( 14 ). Their endpoints and sampling horizon are matched, so only the spectral interpolation changes. Computed from each training fold, the SQ exponent is − 0.79 -0.79 , so the nearest pinned clock, a ¯ = − 0.83 \bar{a}=-0.83 , is the SQ arm. Standard VP uses the same body with scalar preconditioning. On METR-LA, we compare the covariance GSO with the Laplacian GSO 𝐒 = σ 2 ​ ( 𝐋 + γ ​ 𝐈 ) − 1 {\mathbf{S}}=\sigma^{2}({\mathbf{L}}+\gamma{\mathbf{I}})^{-1} . Here, 𝐋 = 𝐈 − 𝐃 − 1 / 2 𝐖𝐃 − 1 / 2 {\mathbf{L}}={\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}{\mathbf{W}}{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} is the normalized Laplacian of the road graph, with 𝐖 {\mathbf{W}} the symmetrized sensor adjacency of [ 14 ] and 𝐃 {\mathbf{D}} its degree matrix. We set γ ≈ 0.02 \gamma\approx 0.02 and choose σ 2 \sigma^{2} so that both GSOs have the same trace. Their SQ exponents are − 0.97 -0.97 and − 1.18 -1.18 , respectively. We also evaluate the GAD model of [ 19 ] on METR-LA. Training and evaluation. All controlled colored and VP arms use the same bias-free GNN with J = 3 J=3 graph-convolution blocks, filter order K = 5 K=5 , width n ch = 96 n_{\mathrm{ch}}=96 , SiLU nonlinearities, and scale-only FiLM conditioning. We train all colored and VP models using an Adam optimizer at a flat learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} for 8 × 10 4 8\times 10^{4} updates. We found naive Euler–Maruyama integration to handle the stiffness of ( 5 ) poorly. We instead discretize on a geometric time grid with a Heun solver [ 10 ] for the probability-flow (PF) ODE [ 22 ] and an ancestral sampler [ 8 ] . For each generated cloud, we report two metrics against the fold’s held-out frames and normalize each by the score of an exact Gaussian draw with the fold’s training covariance, which we call the oracle. The first of these is the relative covariance error. The second is the average maximum mean discrepancy (aMMD) over the quadratic variation, degree correlation and spectral centroid descriptors of closely related works [ 19 , 20 ] . Findings. Table 1 quantifies the main advantage of the colored construction, which is that it requires fewer sampling steps N N to reach a generation quality on par with or better than standard diffusion. On fMRI at twenty ancestral steps, every colored arm outperforms standard VP on both metrics, and by a wide margin. At twenty Heun steps, the gap is smaller. On METR-LA the colored arms lead only at twenty ancestral steps. Notably, the Laplacian GSO remains competitive despite its stationarity mismatch. We found GAD to trail standard VP in every column. Given that whitened VP already captures most of the low-step gain on fMRI, we conclude that the colored prior and Wiener head are the main contributors and the clock exponent is a smaller and less uniform refinement. The steepest clock is the best arm at twenty ancestral steps and beats the whitened member on every fold. Yet, this ordering does not generalize across the table where the pinned exponents lie within one another’s fold variation. The SQ arm, which a spectral-quantile criterion selects without reference to these outcomes, is competitive in every column and is never the worst colored arm. Fig. 1 compares the colored model pinned at the spectral-quantile exponent a ¯ = − 0.83 \bar{a}=-0.83 with standard VP on fMRI across both samplers and all step budgets. All reported metrics are averaged across the five held-out folds. In Fig. 1 (a), the colored arm reaches the covariance-matched reference at ten probability-flow steps and at fifty ancestral steps, and it does not move as N N grows further. Standard VP starts at twice the reference under probability flow and at three times under the ancestral sampler, and needs two hundred steps or more to reach it. The paired aMMD contrast in Fig. 1 (b) has the same shape. Under the probability-flow solver it stays positive on every fold through one hundred steps, while under the ancestral sampler it is far larger at ten and twenty steps and has closed by fifty. Since the arms coincide at the largest budgets, coloring changes how many steps second-order structure costs rather than what is recovered in the limit. Finally, Fig. 1 (c) shows where the cost is paid. At fifty Heun steps, standard VP retains about half of the held-out variance in the middle bands and exceeds it in the roughest ones, whereas the colored model reproduces its training variance in every band to within five percent.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusions
sections.text: We proposed a family of graph-colored, score-based diffusions for stationary graph signals. It gives several existing diffusions a common spectral reading and exposes the spectral inductive bias as a single tunable clock. The prior is colored by the GSO, and the denoiser splits into an analytic Wiener head and a learned GNN body. On fMRI and traffic data, the gain of the colored design is largest at low sampling step counts. We leave the stability analysis of colored diffusions and their task-adaptive optimization to future work.

They inherit a coarse-to-fine generation hierarchy from the nonuniform data spectrum, because each frequency band loses signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at its own rate. For signals on a graph, the relevant spectrum is that of the graph shift operator (GSO). A natural construction, therefore, builds both the diffusion dynamics and the denoiser from graph filters of the GSO, and any such design also takes a position on this hierarchy. We expose this hierarchy as a tunable axis through a family of colored score-based diffusions. Fixing the terminal prior to a Gaussian colored by the GSO couples the drift and diffusion through a positive spectral rate, which acts as a clock for each graph-frequency band. The clock sets when a band loses and recovers information, and the forward processes of standard and certain graph-aware diffusions appear as members of this family. A GSO-valued EDM preconditioning splits the denoiser into an analytic Wiener head that carries the Gaussian second-order structure and a graph neural network (GNN) that learns the remaining non-Gaussian dependencies. Numerical experiments show that colored diffusions reach a given generation quality in far fewer sampling steps than standard diffusion. Index Terms: Diffusion models, spectral bias, stochastic graph signals, graph neural networks † † address: Dept. of Electrical and Systems Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA 1 Introduction Signals defined on graph-structured domains arise in sensor, traffic, financial, and physiological applications [ 16 ] . Recent works generate such signals with diffusion or flow models, incorporating the graph topology through graph neural network parametrizations of the learned dynamics [ 23 , 24 , 19 , 20 ] . The forward process itself, however, has largely remained isotropic. These models, therefore, barely exploit the spectral anisotropy that is inherent to diffusion models and that the graph also supplies. The inherent anisotropy is visible in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Standard diffusion injects spectrally flat (white) noise, whereas smooth graph signals and many natural signal modalities concentrate their energy at low to moderate frequencies [ 25 ] . High-frequency components, therefore, become noise-dominated earlier and are recovered later by the reverse (generative) process [ 7 , 18 ] . Standard diffusion thus inherits a coarse-to-fine generation hierarchy from the data spectrum. This is often a useful inductive bias, but it is determined by the spectral energy distribution rather than being tailored to the generation task. This motivates treating the spectral hierarchy as a design choice. Graph-aware diffusions (GAD) [ 19 ] advance both the spectral and graph-aware axes together. They combine a time-warped heat process with a Laplacian-parametrized Gaussian Markov random field prior and read the reverse process as graph signal denoising. The Fourier-space analysis of [ 7 ] relates unequal frequency SNRs to high-frequency generation errors and proposes EqualSNR diffusion to reduce this imbalance. Blurring, heat-dissipation, and fitted spectral schedules provide related alternatives in image, covariance, and prescribed transform bases [ 18 , 9 , 4 , 26 , 13 , 2 ] . In this paper, we introduce a family of colored diffusions for approximately stationary graph signals on symmetric graph shift operators (GSOs). The GSO may encode known graph structures or be estimated from data, as in covariance graphs. We fix the high-noise prior to a Gaussian whose covariance is colored by the graph operator. This ties the drift and diffusion, and leaves one functional degree of freedom, a positive spectral rate that acts as a clock for each graph-frequency band and determines when that band loses and recovers information. The hierarchy thus becomes a design choice decoupled from the prior while standard diffusion and the GAD processes become special cases with a common spectral reading. The same principle applies to our denoiser design. Matrix-valued EDM preconditioning yields an analytic Wiener head for the Gaussian second-order structure, leaving a nonlinear graph neural network (GNN) body to learn the remaining non-Gaussian and cross-frequency dependencies. Notably, every forward, preconditioning, and reverse operator is a matrix function of the graph shifts that can be applied by matrix–vector products without eigendecomposition. On fMRI and METR-LA datasets, we present extensive ablations across clock shapes, graph shifts, and sampling budgets. We demonstrate that spectral coloring improves low-step generation. We instead discretize on a geometric time grid with a Heun solver [ 10 ] for the probability-flow (PF) ODE [ 22 ] and an ancestral sampler [ 8 ] . For each generated cloud, we report two metrics against the fold’s held-out frames and normalize each by the score of an exact Gaussian draw with the fold’s training covariance, which we call the oracle. The first of these is the relative covariance error. The second is the average maximum mean discrepancy (aMMD) over the quadratic variation, degree correlation and spectral centroid descriptors of closely related works [ 19 , 20 ] . Findings. Table 1 quantifies the main advantage of the colored construction, which is that it requires fewer sampling steps N N to reach a generation quality on par with or better than standard diffusion. On fMRI at twenty ancestral steps, every colored arm outperforms standard VP on both metrics, and by a wide margin. At twenty Heun steps, the gap is smaller. On METR-LA the colored arms lead only at twenty ancestral steps. Notably, the Laplacian GSO remains competitive despite its stationarity mismatch. We found GAD to trail standard VP in every column. Given that whitened VP already captures most of the low-step gain on fMRI, we conclude that the colored prior and Wiener head are the main contributors and the clock exponent is a smaller and less uniform refinement. The steepest clock is the best arm at twenty ancestral steps and beats the whitened member on every fold. Yet, this ordering does not generalize across the table where the pinned exponents lie within one another’s fold variation. The SQ arm, which a spectral-quantile criterion selects without reference to these outcomes, is competitive in every column and is never the worst colored arm. Fig. 1 compares the colored model pinned at the spectral-quantile exponent a ¯ = − 0.83  ar{a}=-0.83 with standard VP on fMRI across both samplers and all step budgets. All reported metrics are averaged across the five held-out folds. In Fig. 1 (a), the colored arm reaches the covariance-matched reference at ten probability-flow steps and at fifty ancestral steps, and it does not move as N N grows further. Standard VP starts at twice the reference under probability flow and at three times under the ancestral sampler, and needs two hundred steps or more to reach it. The paired aMMD contrast in Fig. 1 (b) has the same shape. Under the probability-flow solver it stays positive on every fold through one hundred steps, while under the ancestral sampler it is far larger at ten and twenty steps and has closed by fifty. Since the arms coincide at the largest budgets, coloring changes how many steps second-order structure costs rather than what is recovered in the limit. Finally, Fig. 1 (c) shows where the cost is paid. At fifty Heun steps, standard VP retains about half of the held-out variance in the middle bands and exceeds it in the roughest ones, whereas the colored model reproduces its training variance in every band to within five percent. 5 Conclusions We proposed a family of graph-colored, score-based diffusions for stationary graph signals. It gives several existing diffusions a common spectral reading and exposes the spectral inductive bias as a single tunable clock. The prior is colored by the GSO, and the denoiser splits into an analytic Wiener head and a learned GNN body. On fMRI and traffic data, the gain of the colored design is largest at low sampling step counts.
